newsitem.title: USA: Millions to help FDA enforce tobacco rule.
newsitem.headline: Millions to help FDA enforce tobacco rule.

text.p: Millions of volunteers are ready to help the Food and Drug Administration enforce its first phase of regulations aimed at reducing underage smoking set to take effect Friday, anti-smoking officials said Wednesday.

On Friday, retailers across the country will be required to check photo identification of anyone buying tobacco products who appears younger than 27. The regulations establish 18 as the minimum age for buying tobacco.
The rules allow anyone to report illegal sales to the FDA through a toll-free number and anti-smoking advocacy groups have organized teams of citizens to check on retailers.

During a telephone news conference held by the National Center for Tobacco-Free Kids that included the Attorney General of Indiana and Florida's director of Alcoholic Beverages and Tobacco Enforcement, officials said the volunteers were ready to assist in enforcing the rule.

"We do have an army of literally millions of volunteers around the country belonging to the major health organizations who will be on the lookout for retailers who flout the law," said Matthew Myers, executive vice president and general counsel of the National Center for Tobacco-Free Kids.
"I think it will be the volunteers who will be the major eyes and ears of the FDA but the FDA does plan to use some of its own investigators to get out in the field quickly," he said.

This spring, the FDA will contract with state agencies in 10 states to conduct compliance checks. Teens, accompanied by state or local officials, will visit stores and attempt to buy cigarettes and smokeless tobacco.
Within a year, the agency hopes to have contracts with agencies in all 50 states. The 10 states have not yet been chosen.

Retailers found to violate the law on the first round of checks will receive a warning letter. Those who fail a second check will be fined $250. Fines will increase for subsequent violations and can reach as much as $15,000.
The FDA is planning to post the results of the compliance checks on its Website and will list the names of the retail outlets involved.
The identification checks are part of more comprehensive package of rules that are being challenged by the tobacco industry.
Although the rules cover cigarettes and smokeless tobacco, they exclude cigars.

"Perhaps cigars should be covered but they are not covered because there is not the breadth of information about the manipulation of nicotine in cigars," Myers said. "Therefore there isn't the evidence that would justify FDA assertion of jurisdiction."
The tobacco industry maintains that nicotine is not addictive and denies allegations that it manipulates the level of nicotine in cigarettes to keep smokers hooked.
Earier this month a federal judge in Greensboro, N.C., heard the industry's arguments that the FDA rules should be thrown out.
The judge is expected to be the first to rule on whether the FDA has the right to regulate cigarette sales and marketing and whether the proposed rules are constitutional.

Although the identification requirement is set to begin Friday, the bulk of the rules are to be phased in by this August and August of 1998. Those rules would restrict advertising in some publications, ban free samples and billboard ads near schools and playgrounds, limit vending machine sales, ban sponsorship of sports events and the use of cigarette brands on hats, T-shirts and other products.
